    Fine Arts Survey · The Baroque Period, Part 1 of 3

    From Renaissance to BaroqueDrama, Spectacle, and the Rise of the Violin

    Today’s question: How did the arts become bigger, bolder, and more dramatic as the Renaissance gave way to the Baroque?

    Escape code

    Setting the Scene

    The Renaissance lasted from about 1400 to 1600. The Baroque era followed, from about 1600 to 1750. An era is a long stretch of history that has its own style and ideas.

    The name Baroque may come from a Portuguese word for an oddly shaped pearl. At first, critics used it as an insult for art they thought was too fancy and over-the-top!

    Renaissance art valued calm, balance, and harmony. Baroque art wanted to stir up people’s emotions. In every art form, Baroque artists loved drama, contrast, movement, and decoration. Contrast means putting very different things side by side, like light next to dark or loud next to soft.

    Kings, queens, and the Church

    Kings, queens, and the Church used grand art, music, and performances to show their power and inspire awe. The Baroque period is also called the “age of absolutism,” because many rulers had absolute power, meaning total control over the people they ruled. In France, King Louis XIV turned court life into a constant show of palaces, ballets, operas, and plays.

    Even great musicians worked for these powerful rulers, almost like servants. In Germany, a duke could throw his court musician, Johann Sebastian Bach, into jail for a month because Bach stubbornly asked to leave his job.

    Europe was also divided by religion. France, Spain, Italy, and Austria were mostly Catholic. England, Holland, Denmark, Sweden, and parts of Germany were mostly Protestant. Churches of both kinds used emotional, theatrical art and music to make worship more moving.

    A world of new ideas

    This was also an age of science. Galileo improved the telescope and studied the moons of Jupiter, and Isaac Newton discovered mathematical laws that explain how things move. Ideas that sound normal today, like Earth moving around the Sun, were still controversial. In 1633, Galileo was put on trial for teaching that idea.

    A growing middle class of merchants and doctors, especially in Holland, began buying art too. They wanted paintings of real landscapes and everyday life, not just kings and saints.

    Art History: Two Styles, Two Davids

    Renaissance art: the “gold standard”

    Renaissance artists such as Leonardo da Vinci, Michelangelo, and Raphael wanted their work to look real and perfectly balanced. For centuries, people treated Renaissance art as the gold standard, the model all other art was measured against.

    What does “Baroque” mean?

    Like many names for art periods, Baroque started out as an insult. It described a strange, bizarre taste that didn’t follow the rules of classical art, the art of ancient Greece and Rome that Renaissance artists admired. Baroque art grew out of the classical tradition, but it also reacted against it.

    The Baroque era also looked different from country to country. In the 1600s, modern nations were taking shape, so Baroque art in Italy, France, and Holland each followed its own set of rules.

    Six ways to tell them apart

    An art historian named Heinrich Wölfflin created a famous way to compare the two styles, using pairs of opposites:

    RenaissanceBaroque
    1. LinesLinear: every outline is clear, and the paint is smooth (Raphael)Painterly: outlines are hard to see, shapes disappear into shadow, and brushstrokes are loose (Caravaggio, Peter Paul Rubens)
    2. LightClear, even light shows every part of the pictureLight comes from one focused source and leaves other areas in darkness (Rembrandt’s The Night Watch)
    3. SpaceFigures are lined up across the front, like actors on a stage (Giotto’s Lamentation)The scene moves back into deep space (landscapes by Nicolas Poussin)
    4. FormClosed: balanced, calm, and poisedOpen: full of energy and motion
    5. PartsMany separate details, each complete on its own (Hugo van der Goes’s Portinari Altarpiece)All the parts blend together and can’t be separated (Artemisia Gentileschi’s dramatic Bible scenes)
    6. TimeTimeless: one scene sums everything up (Raphael’s The School of Athens)Dramatic: we see a moment of action as it happens (Rubens’s The Fall of Phaeton)

    Put all six pairs together, and you get a static, or still, Renaissance and a dynamic, or moving, Baroque.

    The dramatic contrast of light and dark in Baroque painting is called chiaroscuro (kee-ar-oh-SKOO-roh), Italian for “light-dark.” When the darkness is extremely deep and the light very sharp, it’s called tenebrism (TEN-uh-briz-um), as in the paintings of Georges de La Tour.

    Two Davids

    A famous example is the statue of David, the young hero from the Bible who fought the giant Goliath.

    Michelangelo’s David (Renaissance) stands balanced, calm, and poised. He is gathering his courage before the fight.

    Bernini’s David (Baroque) is coiled like a spring in an open stance, about to launch his stone. A Renaissance statue usually has one best viewing angle, but Bernini’s David makes you walk all the way around it to take in the action.

    Try it

    Renaissance or Baroque?

    Read each description and choose the style it describes. A wrong answer pauses the buttons while you reread the passage that explains it.

    1. Outlines are hard to see and brushstrokes are loose.
    2. Clear, even light shows every part of the picture.
    3. The scene moves back into deep space.
    4. Balanced, calm, and poised: a “closed” form.
    5. We see a moment of action as it happens.
    6. A statue with one best viewing angle.

    A word of caution

    Not every Renaissance or Baroque artwork fits neatly into all six categories. A style is a very broad label, so to truly understand an artwork, you also need to know the artist’s role, the purpose of the art, and the country and time it came from.

    What came next

    The Baroque style lasted a long time, well into the 1700s, and in France it changed into the lighter Rococo style. Some historians once looked down on the Baroque. The scholar Jacob Burckhardt called it a decline from classical art, and his ideas inspired Wölfflin’s comparison of the two styles.

    Connection

    Chiaroscuro has a twin in music. Baroque composers loved terraced dynamics, sudden switches between loud and soft, the way a painter puts bright light right next to deep shadow. You’ll hear this in Room 6.

    Theater History: From the Globe to the Restoration

    Elizabethan theater (1558–1603)

    This period is named for Queen Elizabeth I of England, who loved plays. London built its first public playhouses: one simply called “The Theatre” opened in 1576, and the most famous, the Globe Theatre, was built in 1599 by William Shakespeare’s acting company.

    • The Globe was a round, open-air theater with a thrust stage that stuck out into the audience, so people watched from three sides.
    • Poorer audience members, called groundlings, paid a penny to stand in the yard right next to the stage. Wealthier people sat in covered galleries.
    • There was little scenery, so the words and fancy costumes told the audience where they were. Shows took place in daylight, with no electric lights or microphones.
    • Only men and boys could act, so boys played all the women’s roles.
    • Other famous playwrights included Christopher Marlowe and Ben Jonson.
    Watch on YouTubeElizabethan Theatre Explained: Shakespeare’s Stage and the Globe

    Restoration theater (1660 onward)

    In 1642, England’s Puritan government closed all the theaters because it believed plays were sinful. The Puritans were a strict Protestant group. For 18 years, there was almost no legal theater in England.

    In 1660, King Charles II returned to the throne, an event called the Restoration, and the theaters reopened with big changes:

    • Women acted on stage in England for the first time, and some became celebrities.
    • Theaters moved indoors, with a proscenium arch framing the stage like a picture frame, and painted, movable scenery lit by candles.
    • The most popular plays were comedies of manners: witty comedies poking fun at rich people’s gossip, fashion, and showing off.
    • Aphra Behn became one of the first English women to earn a living as a writer.

    Try it

    Connection

    When the theaters reopened, they needed music. Henry Purcell, often called the greatest English composer, wrote songs, dances, and overtures for spoken plays in Restoration London, along with his opera Dido and Aeneas.

    Theater Around the World

    While Shakespeare’s plays filled the Globe, other parts of the world were creating great theater too. Look for things they share with English theater, and things that are completely different.

    Japan: kabuki

    Around 1603, a performer named Izumo no Okuni began dancing short, lively shows in Kyoto, Japan. Her style became kabuki, a colorful theater of music, dance, and acting with bold makeup and costumes.

    Kabuki was started by a woman, but in 1629 Japan’s government banned women from performing it. After that, men played all the roles. Actors who specialize in women’s roles are called onnagata. Compare this with England, where boys played women’s roles at the Globe!

    Kabuki theaters later added a hanamichi (hah-nah-MEE-chee), a raised walkway that runs right through the audience. Like the Globe’s thrust stage, it brings actors close to the crowd.

    Japan: bunraku puppet theater

    Bunraku is Japanese puppet theater. A chanter tells the story and speaks for every character, a player on the shamisen (a three-string plucked instrument) adds music, and puppeteers move large, detailed puppets in full view of the audience. The playwright Chikamatsu Monzaemon (1653–1725) wrote so many great bunraku plays that he is sometimes called “Japan’s Shakespeare.”

    Spain: the Golden Age

    In Spain, plays were performed in corrales, open-air courtyards between buildings, with balconies and windows for seats. Spain’s greatest playwright of the time, Lope de Vega (1562–1635), claimed to have written about 1,500 plays! Unlike in England, women could act on stage in Spain.

    China: kunqu opera

    In China, a graceful style of sung theater called kunqu (KOON-choo) was popular. Its most famous work, The Peony Pavilion by Tang Xianzu, appeared in 1598. It is so long that a complete performance can take more than 20 hours, spread over several days. Kunqu uses flutes, drums, and very little scenery: a table and two chairs can become a palace, a garden, or a mountain.

    Try it

    Where in the world?

    Connection

    Music is at the heart of all these theaters. Kabuki and bunraku use the shamisen and drums; kunqu singers are accompanied by a bamboo flute. In Europe, the same love of sung drama was giving birth to opera, a play in which the story is sung.

    Dance History: Ballet at the Royal Court

    From Italy to France

    Ballet began in the royal courts of Renaissance Italy, where nobles performed elegant dances at grand celebrations. When Catherine de’ Medici of Florence married into the French royal family, she brought these court dances to France. In 1581, her court presented the Ballet Comique de la Reine, often called one of the first ballets.

    These early shows were court ballets (ballet de cour): ballets performed by nobles at a royal court, mixing dance with poetry, singing, costumes, and scenery. The dancers were courtiers, nobles who lived at the royal court and served the king or queen.

    The Sun King

    Ballet truly took off in the Baroque era under King Louis XIV of France. He loved to dance and performed in court ballets himself. In 1653, at age 14, he danced the role of the rising sun in the Ballet de la Nuit (“Ballet of the Night”), a court ballet that lasted about 13 hours! That role helped earn him his nickname, the Sun King.

    In 1661, Louis founded the Royal Academy of Dance to train dancers and set rules for ballet. It protected the noble style (danse noble), the elegant, dignified way of dancing developed at the French court. A favorite court dance was the minuet, an elegant dance in triple meter (counted in threes) with small, graceful steps.

    His dancing master, Pierre Beauchamp, is credited with the five positions of the feet that ballet dancers still learn today. A ballet master is the person in charge of training dancers and creating ballets, and a choreographer is the person who creates the steps and movements of a dance. The five positions all use turnout: turning the legs outward from the hips, so the feet point to the sides.

    Explore

    The five positions

    Click each position to see how the feet are placed. Stand up and try them!

    First position: heels together, toes turned out to the sides.

    Second position: feet apart about the width of the shoulders, still turned out.

    Third position: the heel of the front foot touches the middle of the back foot.

    Fourth position: one foot in front of the other, about a foot apart, both turned out.

    Fifth position: feet fully crossed, the front heel touching the toes of the back foot.

    Dance steps were even written down. Dance notation is a system of writing dance steps on paper, like sheet music for dancers. A system developed in Louis XIV’s time was published by Raoul-Auger Feuillet in 1700. Because ballet grew up in France, ballet terms like plié, jeté, and pirouette are still in French.

    Jean-Baptiste Lully: the king’s composer

    Jean-Baptiste Lully (1632–1687) was born in Florence, Italy, and came to France as a teenager. He was a talented violinist, dancer, and composer, and he even danced alongside the young Louis XIV in the Ballet de la Nuit. He played with the king’s famous string group, the 24 Violins (you’ll meet them in Room 8), and became the king’s favorite composer, in charge of all the music at the royal court.

    Lully wrote music for dozens of court ballets. Later, he took control of the Royal Academy of Music (the Paris Opéra) and created a new kind of French opera that always included ballet. A section of dances inserted into an opera or play for entertainment is called a divertissement (dee-vair-TEES-mahn). The French also created the opéra-ballet, a show combining singing, dancing, and orchestral music in a series of scenes linked by a loose theme.

    Lully’s death is one of the strangest stories in music history. In his time, conductors kept the beat by pounding a long, heavy staff on the floor. In 1687, while conducting, Lully accidentally struck his own foot with the staff. The wound became badly infected, and he died a few months later.

    Molière: the king’s playwright

    Molière (1622–1673) was the stage name of Jean-Baptiste Poquelin, an actor and playwright and one of the greatest comedy writers in history. His plays poked fun at fakers, snobs, greedy people, and know-it-all doctors. They’re still performed around the world today.

    Lully and Molière together: the comédie-ballet

    Starting in the 1660s, Lully and Molière teamed up to create a brand-new kind of show for Louis XIV’s court: the comédie-ballet, a play that mixes comedy with dance and music. Their most famous comédie-ballet is The Bourgeois Gentleman (Le Bourgeois gentilhomme, 1670). It tells the story of Monsieur Jourdain, a rich man who desperately wants to act like a noble. He hires teachers to give him lessons in music, dance, fencing, and even philosophy, and makes a fool of himself in hilarious ways.

    Listen to an example

    Lully, Overture to The Bourgeois Gentleman (1670)

    This recording comes from an album called The Orchestra of the Sun King. Listen for the slow, proud opening with jerky “long-short” dotted rhythms, then a quicker section where the instruments chase each other. This kind of opening, called a French overture, made the audience feel the king had arrived.

    ⚜️ Louisiana connection

    In 1682, the French explorer La Salle traveled down the Mississippi River and claimed the whole river valley for France. He named it Louisiana (La Louisiane) in honor of King Louis XIV, the same Sun King who danced in the Ballet de la Nuit. Our state’s name comes straight from Baroque France.

    Music History: The Sound of the Baroque

    Baroque music is full of energy, contrast, and decoration. A Baroque piece usually keeps one basic mood all the way through: what begins joyful stays joyful. Listen for these features:

    • Basso continuo: a steady bass line played underneath the music, usually by a cello plus a harpsichord or organ filling in chords. It works like the foundation of a building.
    • Terraced dynamics: the music switches suddenly between loud and soft, like steps on a staircase, rather than slowly getting louder or softer. Dynamics means how loud or soft music is.
    • Ornamentation: extra decorative notes, like trills, added to a melody. A trill is a quick back-and-forth between two neighboring notes.
    • Steady, driving rhythm: a strong beat that keeps moving forward.
    • Major and minor keys: the system of happy-sounding major and sad-sounding minor keys we still use today became standard.

    Why the sudden loud and soft? The main keyboards of the time, the organ and the harpsichord, can’t make a note louder by pressing harder, the way a piano can. A harpsichord plucks its strings with small quills, so players changed volume in steps instead.

    New forms of music

    A form is the type or plan of a piece of music. Baroque composers created new ones:

    • Opera: a play in which the story is sung, born in Italy around 1600. Claudio Monteverdi’s L’Orfeo (1607) is one of the earliest still performed.
    • Concerto: a piece for a solo instrument accompanied by an orchestra, like Antonio Vivaldi’s The Four Seasons.
    • Oratorio: a large work for singers and orchestra on a religious story, performed without costumes or acting, like George Frideric Handel’s Messiah.
    • Fugue: a piece where one melody is copied and layered by different voices, mastered by Johann Sebastian Bach.

    The Baroque orchestra

    A Baroque orchestra had about 10 to 40 players, and the instruments changed from piece to piece. Click each section to learn its job.

    Strings: violins, violas, cellos, and double basses. The violin family was the heart of every Baroque orchestra.

    Basso continuo: a keyboard (harpsichord or organ) plus a low instrument like a cello or bassoon. Together they play the bass line and fill in chords. Every piece has one.

    Woodwinds: recorders, flutes, and oboes. Composers added them when they wanted a special color. An oboe might play the same tune as the violins.

    Brass: trumpets and horns. Baroque trumpets had no valves, so playing them was very hard. Trumpeters were the aristocrats of the orchestra; if captured in war, they were treated like military officers!

    Timpani: large kettle drums, usually played together with the trumpets for festive or royal music.

The French composers it mentions are François Couperin and Jean-Philippe Rameau. The harpsichord was the main keyboard instrument, but the violin family led the orchestra.

    The Rise of the Violin

    The violin first appeared in northern Italy in the early 1500s. It developed from earlier bowed instruments like the rebec and the vielle. The violin family means the string instruments played with a bow: the violin, viola, cello, and double bass.

    Cremona: violin town

    The town of Cremona, Italy, became famous for violin making. Andrea Amati was one of the earliest known violin makers, and later masters like Antonio Stradivari and the Guarneri family made instruments so beautiful that some are worth millions of dollars today.

    A person who builds and repairs string instruments is called a luthier (LOO-tee-er). Stradivari was a luthier who made about 1,100 instruments in his lifetime; about 650 survive today.

    The star of the orchestra

    During the Baroque era, the violin became the star of the orchestra. Its bright, expressive voice could sing a melody like a human voice and also play fast, flashy passages. Antonio Vivaldi was himself a brilliant violinist, and he wrote hundreds of concertos for the instrument.

    Every instrument has its own timbre (TAM-ber): the special “color” or quality of a sound that makes one instrument sound different from another. A violin and a flute can play the same note, yet you can still tell them apart.

    Then and now

    The violin has changed a little since then. Modern violins have a slightly longer, angled neck, strings made of steel or synthetic materials instead of animal gut, and a bow shape perfected in the late 1700s. Those changes give a louder, more powerful sound for large concert halls.

    Explore

    Baroque violin vs. modern violin

    Click each part to compare.

    Neck: Baroque violins had a shorter neck set straight out from the body. Modern violins have a slightly longer, angled neck.

    Strings: Baroque strings were made of animal gut. Modern strings are steel or synthetic materials, which sound louder and brighter.

    Bow: Baroque bows were lighter and often curved outward. The modern bow shape was perfected in the late 1700s.

    Sound: all these changes give modern violins a louder, more powerful sound for large concert halls. Baroque violins sound softer and sweeter.

    Watch on YouTubeWhy Stradivarius violins are worth millions

    In the video, you’ll learn about a surprising experiment. In a double-blind test, top violinists couldn’t reliably tell old Italian violins like Strads from new ones, and many actually preferred the new violins. So why are Strads still so valuable? Part of the answer is history: each one has been passed from player to player for 300 years.

    Connection

    Cremona is also the hometown of Claudio Monteverdi, whose opera L’Orfeo (1607) is one of the first operas still performed. Monteverdi included violins in the orchestra of L’Orfeo, and he later wrote some of the first special effects for strings.

    The King’s 24 Violins: The Orchestra of the Sun King

    All those court ballets needed music, and much of it came from a famous group of string players called Les Vingt-quatre Violons du Roi, French for “The King’s Twenty-Four Violins.” The group was a five-part string ensemble (a group of musicians who perform together) at the French royal court that lasted from 1626 to 1761. It was founded under Louis XIII, Louis XIV’s father, and played music for celebrations and official events at court.

    The name is a little misleading. The group wasn’t 24 violins exactly. It was 24 instruments from the violin family, from small and high to large and low.

    The five parts

    Today, an orchestra’s string section usually has four main parts: first violins, second violins, violas, and cellos, plus double basses. The King’s 24 Violins were organized differently, into five parts:

    French nameSimilar to today’sHow many
    Premier dessus (top part)Violin6
    Haute-contreSmall viola4
    TailleMedium viola4
    QuinteLarge viola4
    Basse de violonCello6
    Total24

    Notice that there were three different viola parts! The three middle instruments were all tuned the same way, but they came in different sizes, which gave each one its own tone color and volume. The basse de violon was a bit bigger than a modern cello and tuned a whole step lower. This five-part sound, with a strong top and bottom and a rich middle, became the signature sound of French Baroque music.

    Explore

    The five parts of the 24 Violins

    Click each part. The gold bar shows how big the instrument was compared with the others.

    Premier dessus (top part): like today’s violin. 6 players. They played the melody on top.

    Haute-contre: like a small viola. 4 players. The highest of the three middle parts.

    Taille: like a medium viola. 4 players. Same tuning as the haute-contre, but a bigger body for a darker color.

    Quinte: like a large viola. 4 players. About the size of a small guitar, but held and bowed like a violin, so players need a shoulder strap.

    Basse de violon: like a cello. 6 players. A bit bigger than a modern cello and tuned a whole step lower: the strong foundation at the bottom.

    The world’s first orchestra?

    For big events, the 24 Violins sometimes played together with the king’s wind players, who performed for hunts, battles, and outdoor celebrations. Some historians consider this combination the world’s first true orchestra in Western music: a large group of musicians playing string, wind, brass, and percussion instruments together. It later played for operas at Versailles under the composer Jean-Baptiste Lully, who had himself been a member of the 24 Violins.

    Life as a royal musician

    Being one of the King’s Violins was a great honor, and it came with strict rules and special rewards. Members needed a spotless reputation and had to be Roman Catholic. In return, they didn’t have to pay taxes, and they were allowed to carry a sword called a rapier, a privilege usually reserved for nobles! The leader of the group even held the title “King of the Violin.”

    Copied across Europe

    Other kings wanted the same magnificent sound. By 1631, King Charles I of England had set up a similar five-part string group of his own, with 14 players instead of 24. His son Charles II, who had spent years in France while England had no king, created an English “Twenty-four Violins” soon after he returned to the throne in 1660. It may be the origin of the “four-and-twenty fiddlers” in the old nursery rhyme about Old King Cole.

    The end of the 24 Violins

    In 1761, the group was broken up because it cost too much money, and its musicians joined the royal chapel’s musicians, who performed religious music.

    The mystery of the vanished violins

    Here’s a puzzle: three of the five instruments disappeared! Why? According to a 2013 report from The World, the answer was the violins made by Antonio Stradivari in Cremona, Italy. These brilliant violins were perfect for showing off as a soloist, so musicians wanted to play them. The old middle-sized instruments of the 24 Violins were made to blend in, not to stand out. A Paris violin maker compared them to an old video game system nobody uses anymore. Many of the old instruments were not saved, and some of the larger ones were cut apart and rebuilt into smaller instruments that fit the new style.

    In modern times, violin maker Antoine Laulhère and violinist Patrick Cohën-Akenine set out to bring the lost sound back. They had no recordings, photos, or even drawings to go on, only sheet music from the time, mentions in old writings, and sometimes a piece of an original instrument. They rebuilt the missing instruments like detectives. They admit they’ll never know for certain if they got the instruments exactly right, but their work lets us hear something close to what the Sun King heard.

    Listen to an example

    The Sun King’s orchestra: Lully, Overture to The Bourgeois Gentleman

    Listen again with “string ears.” Can you hear the bright top part, the strong bass, and the rich, blended middle where the three viola parts live?

    Connections: Big Ideas Across the Arts

    Baroque artists, musicians, dancers, and actors were all chasing the same big ideas. Read the table across each row to see one idea show up in every art form.

    Big ideaArtMusicTheater, opera, and dance
    ContrastChiaroscuro: bright light next to deep shadowTerraced dynamics: sudden loud and softRestoration comedy: witty jokes about very serious-looking rich people
    Motion and energyBernini’s David, caught in the middle of the actionSteady, driving rhythm and fast, flashy violin passagesBallet leaps and turns; kabuki’s bold movement
    Power and spectacleGrand art made to inspire aweThe King’s 24 Violins playing for royal eventsLouis XIV dancing the Sun in court ballets
    Rules and systemsWölfflin’s six pairs of oppositesMajor and minor keys become standardThe five positions and dance notation
    Who can perform?Women artists like Artemisia Gentileschi succeed against the oddsRoyal violinists had to be CatholicBoys at the Globe, men in kabuki, women on the Restoration stage
